scenario_stem:
Wrenford Bakery is a private limited company running 4 bakery shops in Country X, founded 7 years ago by the Wren family. The business made a profit after tax of $210,000 in 2025 and the directors are deciding how to use it. Shareholders have requested a dividend of $58,000 for this year, while the family wants to open a 5th shop costing $260,000. The board holds a $92,000 contingency reserve used only for emergencies.

The directors are comparing two options: reinvesting $152,000 of retained profit towards the 5th shop, or paying the full dividend and financing the expansion later. Two fitting contractors have quoted for the shop fit-out, differing by $18,000, and the new shop is expected to add $95,000 a year to operating profit once trading begins.

questions.question_text: Define 'retained profit'.
questions.model_answer: Retained profit is the profit kept in the business after tax and after dividends or drawings have been paid, available for reinvestment [2].

knowledge_max_2: profit kept within the business
after tax and after dividends/drawings have been paid

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of using retained profit to finance the new shop.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Retained profit is an internal source, so no external lender needs to be approached [k]; the Wren family avoids interest charges on the $260,000 expansion [app]. Advantage 2: Reinvesting keeps ownership and control with the Wren family [k]; the business does not need to issue new shares to open the 5th shop [app].

knowledge_max_2: internal source: no repayment or interest obligation
retains ownership and control, no new shares needed
application_max_2: avoids interest on the $260,000 expansion
no new shares required for the 5th shop

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of reinvesting $152,000 of retained profit in the 5th shop.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Retained profit is limited by past profits [k]; the business made $210,000 after tax and investing $152,000 leaves little surplus, so the $92,000 contingency reserve could be stretched [app] if the opening is delayed [an]. Disadvantage 2: Reinvesting means shareholders may receive no dividend [k]; they were expecting $58,000 this year [app] and missing the payment could damage the Wren family's relationship with shareholders [an].

knowledge_max_2: limited by the amount of past profit retained
opportunity cost: shareholders receive no dividend
application_max_2: $152,000 reinvested out of $210,000 after-tax profit
shareholders expecting $58,000 dividend
analysis_max_2: contingency reserve could be stretched if opening slips
risk of damaging shareholder relationships / future funding support

questions.question_text: Do you think Wrenford Bakery should reinvest $152,000 of retained profit in the 5th shop or pay the dividend? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Reinvesting the $152,000 [k] would fund most of the 5th shop, avoiding outside finance and interest on the $260,000 expansion [app], and the new shop is expected to add $95,000 a year to operating profit, quickly rebuilding the reserves [an]. However, paying the $58,000 dividend [k] rewards shareholders who have backed the business for 7 years and keeps the family shareholders satisfied [app]; the shop could be financed later once the $18,000 difference between the two contractor quotes is resolved [an]. On balance, reinvestment is the stronger choice [eval], because the expected $95,000 extra annual profit is worth more than a one-off $58,000 dividend once the shop is open [eval]; the $92,000 contingency reserve should stay untouched for emergencies.

knowledge_max_2: reinvestment keeps control and avoids external interest
dividends reward and retain shareholders
application_max_2: $152,000 reinvested towards the $260,000 shop cost
$58,000 dividend vs $95,000 expected extra annual profit
analysis_max_2: extra profit rebuilds reserves quickly after opening
delaying expansion keeps options open on the two quotes differing by $18,000
evaluation_max_2: overall justified recommendation weighing dividend against expansion
recommendation references relative size of $95,000 profit vs $58,000 dividend

scenario_stem:
Sundial Soap Co is a start-up making handmade lavender soaps in Country X, founded 11 months ago by two friends, Priya and Dele. They invested $9,000 of their own savings and sales have reached $6,500 a month. To move from the kitchen to a rented workshop they need $24,000 for a curing rack, packaging and raw materials. The workshop would allow batch curing of up to 1,200 bars a month and secure their first stockist order with a boutique chain.

A local lender offers a micro-finance loan of $24,000 at 14% annual interest over 3 years. Separately, a government start-up grant of $8,000 is available only to rural businesses that create 4 local jobs within 2 years. The friends could also delay the move by 6 months and save $3,500 a month from profits.

questions.question_text: Define 'start-up capital'.
questions.model_answer: Start-up capital is the money needed to set up and begin trading a new business, covering items such as premises, equipment and initial stock [2].

knowledge_max_2: money needed to set up and start trading a new business
covers initial assets and early operating costs

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Sundial Soap Co needs start-up capital.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The move to a rented workshop requires physical assets such as the curing rack [k]; without this equipment the soap cannot be cured at the volumes already selling for $6,500 a month [app]. Reason 2: The workshop adds raw materials and packaging costs [k]; the business needs $24,000 before operations can begin outside the home kitchen [app].

knowledge_max_2: capital equipment and premises required to start trading
initial working costs such as materials and stock
application_max_2: curing rack and workshop equipment required
$24,000 needed with sales already at $6,500 a month

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of a micro-finance loan for Sundial Soap Co.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Micro-finance is designed for very small start-ups like Sundial Soap Co [k]; lenders will consider a $24,000 request that banks may treat as too small or too risky for a new business [app]; this gives Priya and Dele access to funds they might otherwise lack [an]. Advantage 2: A micro-finance loan keeps the owners in full control [k]; repaying $24,000 over 3 years at 14% means the friends keep all their shares and decision-making power [app]; the 14% rate is predictable and can be budgeted at about $3,360 a year [an].

knowledge_max_2: micro-finance serves very small or excluded borrowers
loan preserves ownership and control, unlike share issue
application_max_2: $24,000 loan sized for a micro business
3 years at 14% with full ownership retained by the friends
analysis_max_2: access to funds unavailable from banks
predictable repayment of about $3,360 a year aids budgeting

questions.question_text: Do you think Sundial Soap Co should take the micro-finance loan or apply for the government grant? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Taking the micro-finance loan of $24,000 [k] would let the friends move into the workshop now and fulfil the boutique stockist order while sales are $6,500 a month [app]; at 14% over 3 years the interest is about $3,360 a year, roughly $10,080 in total, which strong sales could absorb [an]. Applying for the $8,000 government grant [k] would bring money that never needs repaying and could create the 4 local jobs required [app]; however it would cover only a third of the $24,000 needed, forcing a long delay or other finance anyway [an]. On balance, the business should take the micro-finance loan and pursue the grant at the same time [eval], because delaying the move by 6 months to save $3,500 a month sacrifices the boutique order and the chance of the $8,000 grant [eval].

knowledge_max_2: loan provides immediate full funding but costs interest
grant is free money but conditional and smaller
application_max_2: $24,000 covers the full workshop move at $6,500 monthly sales
$8,000 grant needs 4 local jobs and covers only part of the cost
analysis_max_2: about $3,360 a year interest (roughly $10,080 over 3 years) is absorbable
grant alone is insufficient, cover only a third of need
evaluation_max_2: overall recommendation weighing interest cost against grant conditions
recommendation considers the cost of delaying six months

scenario_stem:
Boxhaven Packaging Ltd is a private limited company making cardboard boxes for 3 food manufacturers in Country X. Last year the business earned operating profit of $185,000 and it holds $140,000 in retained profit. The directors want to buy a $160,000 box-folding machine, which would raise output by 25% and cut labour costs by $2,800 a month. One of the food manufacturers accounts for 60% of sales, and demand is rising ahead of the busy season.

Wages and raw materials absorb $48,000 a month, and the business must always keep enough cash for the next payroll. The directors must choose between buying the machine now, draining most of the retained profit, or delaying the purchase by 12 months while the balance rebuilds through monthly profits of about $15,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'capital expenditure'.
questions.model_answer: Capital expenditure is spending on non-current assets that will benefit the business for more than one year, such as machinery, vehicles and buildings [2].

knowledge_max_2: spending on long-term / non-current assets
assets used for more than one year

questions.question_text: Explain two needs for finance that Boxhaven Packaging Ltd has.
questions.model_answer: Need 1: The $160,000 box-folding machine is capital expenditure [k]; buying it now would raise output by 25% and cut labour costs by $2,800 a month [app]. Need 2: Day-to-day running costs must still be met [k]; wages and raw materials absorb $48,000 a month, so the business needs working capital to cover every payroll [app].

knowledge_max_2: capital expenditure need: long-term asset purchase
working capital need: day-to-day running costs
application_max_2: $160,000 machine raising output by 25% with $2,800 monthly labour saving
$48,000 a month on wages and raw materials must be covered

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of using retained profit to buy the machine now.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Spending the $140,000 retained profit leaves almost no internal cushion [k]; with wages and raw materials costing $48,000 a month, one late payment from the largest customer could strain the payroll [app], forcing the directors to borrow quickly at short notice [an]. Disadvantage 2: Buying now commits the business before the busy season is fully tested [k]; if orders from the 3 food manufacturers soften, the extra 25% capacity may go unused [app], wasting part of the $160,000 outlay [an].

knowledge_max_2: drains internal funds, leaving little reserve for working capital
commits capital before demand is confirmed
application_max_2: $140,000 retained profit against $48,000 monthly wage and material costs
extra 25% capacity relies on the 3 food manufacturers
analysis_max_2: late customer payment could force emergency short-term borrowing
unused capacity would waste part of the $160,000 spent

questions.question_text: Do you think Boxhaven Packaging Ltd should buy the box-folding machine now or delay 12 months? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying now [k] would capture the $2,800 monthly labour saving, about $33,600 a year, and raise output by 25% precisely when the busy season arrives [app]; with operating profit of $185,000 last year, the extra capacity could be funded from retained profit without external borrowing [an]. Delaying 12 months [k] would let the retained profit balance rebuild through monthly profits of about $15,000, keeping the payroll safe [app]; however, the business would forgo the full year of labour savings, roughly $33,600, and risk disappointing the largest customer that accounts for 60% of sales [an]. On balance, the business should buy now [eval], because the annual saving and protected customer base outweigh the strain on reserves, provided a separate payroll buffer is ring-fenced [eval].

knowledge_max_2: buying now gains labour savings and capacity immediately
delaying preserves working capital and internal reserves
application_max_2: $2,800 a month labour saving (about $33,600 a year) with 25% more output
$185,000 operating profit vs $140,000 retained profit and monthly payroll protection
analysis_max_2: extra capacity matches rising demand and the largest 60%-of-sales customer
delaying forgoes about $33,600 of labour savings over the year
evaluation_max_2: overall justified judgement balancing savings against reserve risk
recommendation references the trade-off with a ring-fenced payroll buffer

scenario_stem:
Indigo Barbers is a sole-trader barber shop in Country X run by Danilo Petrov for 5 years. The shop has one barber chair, and Danilo recently completed a barbering course costing $800. He now wants to hire a second barber and add a second chair costing $7,500, serving up to 60 more customers a month at an average spend of $14. The shop is open 6 days a week and loyalty among local customers is strong.

Danilo has $11,000 in personal savings, and the shop holds $4,200 in the business bank account. His wife works part-time and the family rely on those savings as a buffer against illness. The alternative is to fund the second chair gradually from the business account over 6 months and keep his savings untouched.

questions.question_text: Define 'owners' savings'.
questions.model_answer: Owners' savings are the personal money invested in the business by the owner from their own private funds, used to finance business activity without borrowing [2].

knowledge_max_2: personal money invested by the owner
internal source — does not require repayment

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Indigo Barbers of using owners' savings to fund the second chair.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Owners' savings do not need to be repaid with interest [k], so Danilo keeps borrowing costs at zero while the $7,500 chair is paid for [app]. Advantage 2: The money is available immediately [k], so the second chair can be fitted without waiting for the $4,200 business account to build up over time [app].

knowledge_max_2: internal source: no interest or repayment
immediate availability, no approval delays
application_max_2: no interest charged on the $7,500 chair cost
available now rather than relying on the $4,200 business account

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of using owners' savings in this situation.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: Owners' savings are limited in amount [k]; spending $7,500 of the $11,000 leaves Danilo only $3,500, so the family's buffer against illness would be severely reduced [app], which could force withdrawals from the shop at short notice if a crisis hit [an]. Disadvantage 2: Savings represent the reward for past sacrifice and carry an opportunity cost [k]; the family might otherwise use the money for their own security, and $800 has already gone on the barbering course [app], leaving the household with little margin if Danilo fell ill [an].

knowledge_max_2: limited amount of funds available
opportunity cost to the owner's household security
application_max_2: $7,500 of the $11,000 savings leaves only $3,500 for the family buffer
$800 already spent on the barbering course reduces the cushion further
analysis_max_2: reduced illness buffer could force emergency withdrawals from the shop
household exposure increases if Danilo becomes ill

questions.question_text: Do you think Danilo should use his owners' savings to fund the second chair or spread the cost from the business account over 6 months? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Using owners' savings [k] would let Danilo install the second chair immediately and serve up to 60 more customers a month at $14 each, roughly $840 extra revenue a month [app]; the extra takings would restore his $11,000 within about 9 months of opening [an]. Funding the chair gradually from the business account [k] protects the family buffer and keeps the savings intact [app]; however, the account holds only $4,200, so the $7,500 chair would take far longer to fund and the $840 monthly upside would be lost meanwhile [an]. On balance, Danilo should spread the cost from the business account over 6 months and keep his savings untouched [eval], because the family's buffer against illness matters more than gaining a few months of extra revenue [eval].

knowledge_max_2: savings give immediate expansion and faster extra revenue
business account spreading protects personal financial security
application_max_2: $11,000 savings would fund the $7,500 chair immediately with about $840 extra revenue a month
business account holds only $4,200, insufficient for the $7,500 chair
analysis_max_2: extra takings would restore the savings within about 9 months
delay means losing months of the $840 monthly upside while the buffer stays safe
evaluation_max_2: overall justified recommendation balancing growth against household security
judgement reflects the family buffer against illness risk

scenario_stem:
Oldmill Removals is a private limited company in Country X running 3 removal lorries from a warehouse. The business has just won a 3-year supermarket contract worth $240,000 a year, but it must buy a refrigerated lorry costing $95,000 within 18 months of the first delivery. The supermarket pays 60 days after delivery, and Oldmill Removals employs 14 staff.

The directors hold retained profit of $60,000 and own two unused assets: a flatbed trailer valued at $28,000 and a small warehouse unit valued at $70,000. Selling both assets would raise $98,000, while combining retained profit with the trailer sale would raise $88,000, leaving a $7,000 gap. The warehouse unit has stood empty since 2023 and the trailer has not been used for 2 years.

questions.question_text: Define 'sale of existing assets'.
questions.model_answer: Sale of existing assets is an internal source of finance where a business raises money by selling assets it no longer needs, such as old vehicles, equipment or property [2].

knowledge_max_2: raising money by selling unused or unwanted business assets
internal source — funds come from the business itself

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of selling both unused assets to fund the refrigerated lorry.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Selling both assets would raise $98,000 [k], covering the $95,000 lorry in full with $3,000 to spare [app]. Advantage 2: It is an internal source of finance [k], so no interest is paid and the business keeps full ownership while delivering the supermarket contract worth $240,000 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: raises full funding internally without borrowing
no interest or repayment obligation, ownership unchanged
application_max_2: $98,000 raised covers the $95,000 lorry with $3,000 to spare
supermarket contract worth $240,000 a year secured without lender involvement

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of relying on retained profit plus the trailer sale alone.
questions.model_answer: Disadvantage 1: The $88,000 raised falls short of the $95,000 needed for the refrigerated lorry [k], leaving a $7,000 gap that must be found elsewhere [app], which could delay first deliveries and risk the 3-year supermarket contract [an]. Disadvantage 2: Using all $60,000 retained profit removes the safety cushion [k]; with 14 staff and lorry running costs, one major repair or late supermarket payment could force emergency borrowing [app], raising costs precisely when the contract demands reliability [an].

knowledge_max_2: internal funds raised are insufficient to meet the requirement
retained profit acts as a safety cushion that would be exhausted
application_max_2: $88,000 raised vs $95,000 lorre cost, leaving a $7,000 gap
$60,000 retained profit used up, leaving 14 staff and lorries unprotected
analysis_max_2: gap could delay deliveries and put the supermarket contract at risk
emergency borrowing at short notice raises costs and pressure

questions.question_text: Do you think Oldmill Removals should sell both assets or keep the warehouse unit and combine retained profit with the trailer sale? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Selling both assets raises $98,000 [k], covering the $95,000 refrigerated lorry with $3,000 to spare and keeping the $60,000 retained profit untouched [app]; this protects the 14 staff and guarantees the delivery schedule for the supermarket contract worth $240,000 a year [an]. Keeping the warehouse unit [k] preserves a property that might appreciate and provides storage [app]; but it leaves a $7,000 gap on the $88,000 raised, before the supermarket's first payment 60 days after delivery arrives [an]. On balance, selling both assets is the safer decision [eval], because the unit has stood empty since 2023 and the confirmed $240,000 annual contract matters more than a speculative rise in property value [eval].

knowledge_max_2: sale of both assets fully funds the lorry and protects retained profit
keeping the unit preserves a potentially appreciating asset and storage
application_max_2: $98,000 covers the $95,000 lorry with $3,000 to spare; $60,000 retained profit stays intact
keeping the unit leaves $88,000 raised and a $7,000 gap before first payment 60 days later
analysis_max_2: full funding guarantees deliveries for the $240,000 a year contract and 14 staff
first supermarket payment arrives 60 days after delivery, so cash must not be tight
evaluation_max_2: overall justified recommendation weighing unused property against contract security
judgement notes the unit has been empty since 2023

scenario_stem:
Baobab Sewing Cooperative is a rural start-up in Country X founded 8 months ago by 9 women making school uniforms. The cooperative sells 210 uniforms a month at $18 each and wants to buy an industrial sewing machine costing $5,400 to take a contract with a local school for 500 uniforms a term. Demand rises sharply before the autumn term, and the cooperative works from a donated room in the village clinic.

A government enterprise grant of $2,000 is available for rural start-ups that create at least 3 jobs. A micro-finance institution also offers $5,400 over 24 months at 12% annual interest. The cooperative's members have saved $900 so far and add about $300 a month from profits. Members work part-time around farming commitments.

questions.question_text: Define 'micro-finance'.
questions.model_answer: Micro-finance is the provision of very small loans and financial services to people who cannot access traditional bank finance, typically to start or grow a very small business [2].

knowledge_max_2: very small loans for people excluded from bank finance
aimed at micro-businesses and start-ups

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the government enterprise grant for the cooperative.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: The $2,000 grant does not need to be repaid [k], so it directly reduces the amount the cooperative must borrow for the $5,400 machine [app]. Advantage 2: The grant supports rural start-ups that create jobs [k], helping the cooperative fund its plan to hire at least 3 local women when it signs the school contract [app].

knowledge_max_2: grant is not repayable — free funding
grant encourages job creation in rural areas
application_max_2: $2,000 reduces the $5,400 machine cost needing finance
at least 3 local jobs requirement links to the school contract

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of relying only on the cooperative's own savings.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: The members' savings total only $900 [k], exactly one sixth of the $5,400 machine [app], so saving alone cannot fund the school contract in time and the cooperative risks losing the 500-uniform order [an]. Limitation 2: Accumulating savings is slow [k]; even with the $2,000 grant, covering the remaining $3,400 at $300 a month would take about 11 months, and 18 months without the grant [app], by which time the school may have sourced its uniforms elsewhere [an].

knowledge_max_2: savings accumulated are small relative to the requirement
slow accumulation delays the purchase and the contract
application_max_2: $900 saved vs $5,400 machine cost — one sixth of the requirement
$300 a month surplus: about 11 months with the grant, 18 months without
analysis_max_2: school may lose patience and source uniforms elsewhere
500-uniform contract would be lost, undermining the whole plan

questions.question_text: Do you think the cooperative should take the micro-finance loan or wait and save from profits? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Taking the micro-finance loan of $5,400 [k] would let the cooperative buy the machine now and deliver the 500-uniform school contract, worth about $9,000 a term at $18 per uniform [app]; at 12% interest the cost is about $648 a year, manageable against sales of about $3,780 a month, and the machine pays for itself quickly [an]. Waiting to save $300 a month [k] avoids all interest and keeps the cooperative debt-free [app]; but saving the full amount would take 18 months, and even after the $2,000 grant about 11 months, risking the school contract entirely [an]. On balance, the cooperative should take the micro-finance loan and still apply for the $2,000 grant [eval], because the machine's revenue gain far outweighs roughly $1,296 of interest over 2 years [eval].

knowledge_max_2: loan buys the machine immediately and earns revenue sooner
saving is interest-free but slow and risky
application_max_2: $5,400 machine delivers the 500-uniform contract worth about $9,000 a term at $18 each
saving $300 a month takes 18 months (about 11 with the $2,000 grant)
analysis_max_2: $648 a year interest is absorbable against about $3,780 monthly sales
waiting risks losing the contract; interest over 2 years is only about $1,296
evaluation_max_2: overall justified recommendation combining loan and grant application
judgement weighs contract revenue against interest cost

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:
Redwood Retail Group runs 11 discount stores in Country X. It plans two moves this year: a $350,000 refit of its largest store over 18 months and an $80,000 bulk purchase of stock before the December trading season. The largest store employs 85 staff and anchors a regional shopping centre. The business made a profit after tax of $420,000 last year and holds retained profit of $260,000.

The directors must choose between using retained profit for the December stock and funding the refit with a long-term route, or using retained profit for the refit and covering the stock from short-term sources. Suppliers offer 60 days' trade credit on stock, and bank loans for refits are available at 8% annual interest over 6 years.

Reason 2: Short-term finance avoids paying 8% interest for 6 years on a purchase recovered within weeks [k]; the $80,000 stock will generate cash during December, making a 6-year loan wasteful [app].

The finance manager suggests funding the kitchen from retained profit and selling the 2 old shuttle vans for $14,000 towards the new ones.
